'''''General Relativity''''' is a graduate textbook and reference written by the gravitational physicist [[Robert Wald]]. It provides a [[Rigour#Mathematics|mathematically rigorous]] and thorough introduction to [[Albert Einstein]]'s [[General relativity|general theory of relativity]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Trautman |first=Andrzej |date=January 1986 |title=Review: Theodore Frankel, ''Gravitational Curvature: An Introduction to Einstein's Theory'', and Hans Stephani, ''General Relativity: An Introduction to the Theory of the Gravitational Field'', and Robert M. Wald, ''General Relativity'' |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/bulletin-of-the-american-mathematical-society-new-series/volume-14/issue-1/Review--Theodore-Frankel-Gravitational-curvature-an-introduction-to-Einsteins/bams/1183552796.full |journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=152-158}}</ref>

==Overview==
Published by the University of Chicago Press in 1984, the book of almost 500 pages covers many aspects of the theory of General Relativity. It is divided into two parts: Part I covers the fundamentals of the subject, and Part II covers more advanced topics such as causal structure, and quantum effects.<ref name=book>{{Cite book
| title = General Relativity
| last=Wald|first=Robert M. 
| publisher= University of Chicago Press
| url = https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/G/bo5952261.html
}} Printed (1980) {{ISBN|0-226-87033-2}} (paperback), {{ISBN|0-226-87032-4}} (hardcover); [[EPUB]] and [[PDF]] (2010) {{ISBN|978-0-226-87037-3}}</ref> The book uses the [[abstract index notation]] for [[tensors]].<ref name="Finley">[http://physics.unm.edu/Courses/Finley/p581/Booklist.html A Listing of Technical Books for General Relativity]. Daniel Finley. Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of New Mexico. April 1, 2018. Accessed January 18, 2019.</ref> It covers spinors, the [[Variational methods in general relativity|variational-principle formulation]], the initial-value formulation, (exact) [[gravitational wave]]s, singularities, [[Penrose diagram]]s, [[Hawking radiation]], and black-hole thermodynamics.<ref name=":0">[http://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/physics/Administrivia/rel_booklist.html#intro_gr A Guide to Relativity Books]. [[John C. Baez]] et al. University of California, Riverside. September 1998. Accessed January 18, 2019.</ref>

It is aimed at beginning graduate students and researchers.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=book/>{{rp|Preface}} To this end, most of the material in Part I is geared towards an introductory course on the subject, while Part II covers a wide range of advanced topics for a second term or further study. The essential mathematical methods for the formulation of general relativity are presented in Chapters 2 and 3, while more advanced techniques are discussed in Appendices A to C. Wald believes that this is the best way forward because putting all the mathematical techniques at the beginning of the book would prove to be a major obstruction for students, while developing these mathematical tools as they get used would mean they are too scattered to be useful. While the [[Hamiltonian mechanics|Hamiltonian formalism]] is often presented in conjunction with the initial-value formulation, Wald covers these topics independently, with Hamiltonian relegated to the appendix, alongside the [[Lagrangian mechanics|Lagrangian formalism]].<ref name=book/>{{rp|Preface}}

This book uses the <math>(-,+,+,+)</math> [[Sign convention#Relativity|sign convention]] for reasons of technical convenience, with one important exception: in Chapter 13 ''only'', the sign convention is switched to <math>(+,-,-,-)</math> because it is considered easier to treat spinors this way, and this is the most common sign convention used in the literature.<ref name=book/>{{rp|Notation and Conventions}}

Most of the book uses [[Geometrized unit system|geometrized units]], meaning the fundamental natural constants <math>G</math> (Newton's [[gravitational constant]]) and <math>c</math> ([[Speed of light|the speed of light]] in vacuum) are set equal to one, except when predictions that can be tested are made.<ref name=book/>{{rp|Notation and Conventions}}

{{general relativity}}
*'''Part I: Fundamentals'''
**Chapter 1: Introduction
**Chapter 2: [[Manifolds]] and [[Tensor field|Tensor Fields]]
**Chapter 3: [[Curvature]]
**Chapter 4: [[Einstein field equations|Einstein's Equation]]
**Chapter 5: Homogeneous, Isotropic [[Cosmology]]
**Chapter 6: The [[Schwarzschild Solution]]
*'''Part II: Advanced Topics'''
**Chapter 7: Methods for Solving Einstein's Equation
**Chapter 8: [[Causal structure|Causal Structure]]
**Chapter 9: [[Gravitational singularity|Singularities]]
**Chapter 10: [[Initial value formulation (general relativity)|Initial Value Formulation]]
**Chapter 11: [[Asymptotic flatness|Asymptotic Flatness]]
**Chapter 12: [[Black Holes]]
**Chapter 13: [[Spinors]]
**Chapter 14: [[Quantum field theory in curved spacetime|Quantum Effects in Strong Gravitational Fields]]
*'''Appendices'''
**A. [[Topological space|Topological Spaces]]
**B. [[Differential form|Differential Forms]], Integration, and [[Frobenius theorem (differential topology)|Frobenius's Theorem]]
**C. Maps of Manifolds, [[Lie derivative|Lie Derivatives]], and [[Killing vector field|Killing Fields]]
**D. [[Conformal transformation|Conformal Transformations]]
**E. [[Variational methods in general relativity|Lagrangian and Hamiltonian Formulations of Einstein's Equation]]
**F. Units and Dimensions.

== Assessment ==
Hans C. Ohanian, who taught and researched gravitation at the [[Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute]], opined in 1985 that ''General Relativity'' provided a modern introduction to the subject with emphasis on tensor and topological methods and offers some "sharp insights." However, its quality is very variable. Topics such as [[Schwarzschild geodesics|geodetic motion in the Schwarzschild metric]], the [[Kruskal–Szekeres coordinates|Krushkal extension]], and [[Penrose process|energy extraction from black holes]], are handled well, while empirical tests of Einstein's theory are barely touched; and the treatment of advanced topics, including cosmology, is just too brief to be useful to students. Due to its heavy use of higher mathematics, it may not be suitable for an introductory course.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ohanian|first=Hans|date=September 1985|title=''General Relativity''|department=Book Reviews|journal=American Journal of Physics|publisher=Association of American Physics Teachers|volume=53|issue=9|pages=923–4|doi=10.1119/1.14379|bibcode=1985AmJPh..53..923W}}</ref>

[[Lee Smolin]] argued in 1986 that ''General Relativity'' bridges the gap between the presentation of the material in older textbooks and the literature. For example, while the early pioneers of the subject, including Einstein himself, employed coordinate-based methods, researchers since the mid-1960s had switched to coordinate-free formulations, on which Wald's text is entirely based. Its style is uniformly clear and economical, if too brief at times. Topics that deserve more attention include [[gravitational radiation]] and [[cosmology]]. However, this book could be supplemented by those by Misner, Thorne, and Wheeler, and by Weinberg. Smolin was teaching a course on general relativity to undergraduates as well as graduate students at [[Yale University]] using this book, and felt satisfied with the results. He also found it useful as a reference to refresh his memory.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Smolin |first=Lee |date=January–February 1986 |title=Review: ''General Relativity'' by Robert Wald |journal=American Scientist |volume=74 |issue=1 |page=82 |jstor=27853954}}</ref>

[[Andrzej Trautman]] praised the book for skillfully applying tensor calculus and local differential geometry, and for containing materials not otherwise available in book form at the time of its publication. He further noted that Wald discussed further mathematical methods for relativity in the appendices, unlike other authors of the era.<ref name=":1" />

Theoretical physicist [[James W. York]] commented in 1987 that ''General Relativity'' was a sophisticated yet concise book on the subject that should be appealing to the mathematically inclined, as a high level of rigor is maintained throughout the book. However, he considered the material on [[linearized gravity]] too short, and recommended ''[[Gravitation (book)|Gravitation]]'' by [[Charles W. Misner|Charles Misner]], [[Kip Thorne]], and [[John Archibald Wheeler]], and ''Gravitation and Cosmology'' by [[Steven Weinberg]] as supplements.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=York |first=James |date=May 1987 |title=Review: ''General Relativity'' |department=Books |journal=Physics Today |publisher=American Institute of Physics |volume=40 |issue=5 |pages=94–95 |bibcode=1987PhT....40e..94W |doi=10.1063/1.2820032}}</ref>

In their [[Foreword]] to the ''Feynman Lectures on Gravitation'', [[John Preskill]] and Kip Thorne recommended ''General Relativity'' by Wald as a pedagogically effective and modern introduction to the subject, with an emphasis on its geometric nature.<ref name=":20">{{Cite book |last=Feynman |first=Richard |title=Feynman Lectures on Gravitations |last2=Morinigo |first2=Fernando B. |last3=Wagner |first3=William G. |publisher=Westview |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-813-34038-8 |editor-last=Hatfield |editor-first=Brian |location=Boulder, Colorado |chapter=Foreword by John Preskill and Kip Thorne |chapter-url=http://www.theory.caltech.edu/~preskill/pubs/preskill-1995-feynman.pdf}}</ref>

Nelson Christensen and Thomas Moore put ''General Relativity'' by Wald in the same category as ''Gravitation and Cosmology'' by Weinberg as well as ''Gravitation'' by Misner, Thorne, and Wheeler, noting that these are all mathematically sophisticated graduate-level texts on the subject.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Christensen |first=Nelson |last2=Moore |first2=Thomas |date=2012 |title=Teaching general relativity to undergraduates |url=https://physicstoday.aip.org/features/teaching-general-relativity-to-undergraduates |journal=Physics Today |volume=65 |issue=6 |pages=41-7 |doi=10.1063/PT.3.1605}}</ref>

In his 2018 review, Daniel Finley, a professor at the [[University of New Mexico]], said this textbook was written by a person with good physical intuition. However, the author did not use the most modern mathematical methods available, and his treatment of cosmology had become outdated. Finley deemed the abstract index notation difficult to learn, though convenient for those who had mastered it.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Finley |first=Daniel |date=April 1, 2018 |title=A List of Technical Books on General Relativity |url=https://physics-old.unm.edu/Courses/Finley/p581/Booklist.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240320103950/https://physics.unm.edu/Courses/Finley/p581/Booklist.html |archive-date=March 20, 2024 |access-date=December 23, 2025 |website= |publisher=Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of New Mexico}}</ref>
